report:
## Verdict: The claim is largely overstated — evidence is mixed, not clearly supportive of a strong vegetarian survival advantage

The claim that vegetarian diets increase life expectancy compared with eating meat is **not well supported as a strong, causal effect**, though evidence is genuinely mixed rather than clearly false.

**Evidence against a robust effect:** A recent meta-analysis found vegetarian diets reduced ischemic heart disease mortality but had **no significant effect on all-cause mortality** compared to non-vegetarian diets, with the authors cautioning that certainty of evidence was low ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34611632](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34611632/)). Similarly, the large EPIC-Oxford cohort found overall mortality among British vegetarians was comparable to non-vegetarians, both being lower than general population rates — suggesting a "healthy volunteer" effect rather than a diet-specific benefit ([ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(23)23833-2](https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(23)23833-2/pdf)).

**Evidence for a modest effect:** The Adventist Health Study 2 (73,308 participants) did find vegetarians had lower all-cause mortality than non-vegetarians, though effects were stronger in males and mainly reduced deaths at younger ages ([jamanetwork.com/1710093](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/1710093); [ajcn.nutrition.org/S0002-9165(24)00652-X](https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(24)00652-X/fulltext)).

**Key methodological concern:** Physician and researcher Peter Attia notes that vegetarian-mortality studies are highly susceptible to "healthy user bias" — vegetarians tend to smoke less, exercise more, and be more health-conscious generally, making it difficult to isolate diet as the causal factor ([peterattiamd.com/191027](https://peterattiamd.com/191027/)).

**Conclusion:** The evidence is inconsistent across major cohorts and meta-analyses. Some studies show modest mortality benefits, others show none, and confounding by lifestyle factors remains a major unresolved issue. The claim is an oversimplification of a genuinely contested area of nutritional epidemiology.
